→ Their sleek leggings are the creative.

→ Top themes: Promotion/discount, features/benefits, seasonal

And static ads let them: 
- Show the product exactly how it looks
- Test more colorways and styles faster
- Capture intent from people who already want premium activewear (they don't need to convince you yoga pants are worth buying. They need to convince you their yoga pants are the ones you want) 

IL MAKIAGE
→ 20% static (189 ads)
→ 80% video (1617 ads) 

They sell a transformation: 
→ Foundation that makes you look beautiful 
→ Top angles: Easy application, natural-looking results, perfect match
→ Top themes: Problem & solution, testimonial, before & after

And videos ads let them: 
- Build trust through before and after transformations
- Address skepticism “will this actually work for my skin”
- Walk through their quiz and foundation matching process (their entire funnel is education first, always pushing to a “try before you buy” or “take the quiz”, which struggles to be communicated in a single static image) 

There is no golden bullet when it comes to static vs video. 

Both can be successful. 

But, here’s what I see across all of Meta

Static ads win when: 

The value is visible
→ Fashion
→ Home good
→ Jewelry
→ Food

Video ads win when: 

The value needs proof
→ Skincare results
→ Supplements
→ Subscription services

Bottom line: 
- If the customer needs to SEE IT → Run Statics
- If the needs to BELIEVE IT → Run Videos

Is your media buyer any good? 

Check with 4 simple charts: 

Step 1. Open Meta ads manager
Step 2. Click change log (clock icon top right)
Step 3. Copy last 90 days to a Google Sheet

Then create these charts: 

🔴 Chart 1: When is media buying happening? 

Create a bar chart of media buying changes by day. 

We often see: 
→ 90% of media buying happening on Monday/Thurs or Tues/Friday
→ You’re not getting regular attention on your account

It is very rare that:
- Best time to make changes all appear magically on Monday every week 
- An ad account can go a full day without benefiting from a media buying tweak

And if spending $250k+/mo: 
→ Also check change times as well (how many times per day). 
→ You want to make sure you see full day activity - not just in the mornings or evenings. 

Gold standard you’re looking for is consistent number of changes happening every single day (includes weekends). 

🔴 Chart 2: How big changes are they making? 

Take data from Chart 1 and map the count of positive and negative changes. Categorize into 3% buckets

Three red flags you may see
1. Always the same change, "10%", no matter what the data shows
2. Rarely making changes (you want consistent small optimizations)
3. Often making big changes 50%+/- (destabiizes algorithm)

Example image is gold standard. 
→ Shows an even number of budget decreases and increases
→ Budget changes average around 15% +/-
→ Very rare to see a big budget change of 50% +/-

🔴 Chart 3: Is your Media Buyer making the right decisions? 

Map out the change buckets from Chart 2 vs CPA next day. 
→ When they make bigger changes, does CPA go down? 
→ If yes, should see a downward trending line to the bottom right

If I see a flat trend then that’s also OK. 

But red flag if I see an upward trend
→ This means the bigger the change they make, the higher the CPA goes
→ It means you’re paying your media buyer to run ads badly 

🔴 Chart 4: Who's making changes:

Best media buying results come when only one person makes 90% of decisions. 

I’ve seen too many situations: 
→ Media Buyer 1 works Mon-Thurs and Media Buyer 2 works Fri - Sun
→ Media Buyer changes every 2 months (quitting, staffing etc)
→ Media Buyer & Founder both meddling on account at same time 

🟢 What makes a good media buyer?

They: 
1. Make nuanced changes based on the data
2. Make careful and regular small change
3. Know how ad account responds 
3. Spent lots of time in the ad account

I know Media Buying feels like a black box.

But the best way to judge is to stop measuring a single performance metric (e.g. ROAS / CPA)

And instead measure the process metrics:

→ When are they working 
→ How big changes are they making
→ Are they making the right changes

High MERs might be a bad thing

DTC CFO explained:

Year 1: 
- $20M revenue
- Revenue Mix: 50% organic / 50% paid
- Half of traffic is free. You’re relying on organic. 
- MER: 20% (Looks fantastic - very efficient!)

Then imagine you start spending more on ads

Year 2:
- $50M revenue
- Revenue Mix: 22% organic / 78% paid
- More traffic is paid. You’re using paid ads to grow
- MER: 21.1% (Oh no… it increased)

Here’s what happened: 

1. You worked twice as hard, improved your creative, optimized your funnel, and your efficiency ratio went down.
2. Why? Because you bought a bigger chunk of revenue, your "blended" margin drops.
3. But, because your ROAS improved (from 2.5x to 3.7x, your Net Contribution Dollars (Revenue - COGS - Ad Spend) doubled.
4. So even though MER dropped… you are making more cash. 

Key here is to not optimize for MER.

Instead, optimize for net contribution dollars.

Else you will make the mistake of lowering ad spend to keep MER high.

Is media buying or creative your problem?

I use 9 charts to find out: 

Chart 1: Account Control

→ Maps every ad by CPA vs total spend.
→ Are you cutting losers before they burn cash? 
→ Is your testing structure leaving winning ads unspent? 
→ Are your top 10% of ads generating 50%+ of revenue?

Chart 2: Creative Churn 

→ Tracks how fast your creative inventory turns over relative to performance.
→ Each color = a different month's creative cohort.
→ High churn without performance gains = production issue. 
→ Low churn with declining performance = you're riding old winners too long.

Chart 3: Production & Slugging Rate 

→ How many ads you're launching vs your targets.
→ More importantly: What % are "hits" (spending $5k+)?
→ If only 3/100 ads spend meaningfully, you have a creative quality problem

Chart 4: Performance Trends Basic CPA vs spend over time.

→ Can you scale spend while holding or improving CPA?
→ If your line trends up and right (more spend, worse CPA), you need better creative or better structure.

Chart 5: Creative Allocation 

→ Are you spending the most on your lowest CPA ads?
→ This should be obvious, but most accounts fail here.
→ Your top 1% of ads should drive ~50% of total spend.
→ If your budget is scattered across mediocre performers, your account structure is broken.

Chart 6: Gender/Demo Analysis 

→ Shows who's actually buying vs who you think is buying.
→ Most brands guess at their audience.
→ This chart tells you where to focus production.

Chart 7: Churn/Retesting Control 

→ Darker colors = more new creative testing.
→ Are you dependent on old ads or consistently launching fresh creative.
→ If you see long stretches of light green, you're not testing enough. 
→ If it's all dark with declining performance, you're churning too fast without learning.

Chart 8: Creative Utilization

→ Y-axis: How many placements/audiences per ad 
→ X-axis: Total spend per ad
→ Are you taking your winners and testing them across different audiences, placements & campaign structures
→ Your best ads should have 5+ variations running. 

Chart 9: Spend by Format 

→ Are you producing video/static/UGC in proportion to what actually performs?
→ If 70% of your spend goes to video but you're producing 80% static, you have a production allocation problem.
→ This chart shows the gap between what you make and what works.


The goal is to find data that shows you WHICH problem you actually have:

Is it creative production? 
→ Low hit rate 
→ Poor creative allocation
→ Format mismatch

Or is it media buying? 
→ Bad account control 
→ Poor utilization of winners 
→ Scaling issues

Creative and media buying both drive CPA/ROAS.

Even if they are managed by the same person (they should be) that doesn't give an excuse to blend the metrics.

Measure them separately or you'll fix the wrong thing.

2. Churners → (Adds 500) 

These are users that are projected to hit their full life time value. I’d push back learnings from why old users churned and present education, offers and new products to increase subscription life time before they cancel. This is an evergreen activity that will compound and worth extra attention. 

3. Retained 1 Month → (Adds 500)

These are users that were acquired last month and have been successfully rebilled once. I’m looking to reduce cancellation rate of anyone reaching their first month cliff. I’d over invest into education and value to ensure that new customers get the value they were initially promised. This will be done through email, and paid advertising targeting 1 month customers.

- SCALING ADS: I’d identify all the ads that could have scaled but didn’t. I’d restart them or push more ad spend behind them. The top 1-2% of your ads should take 50%+ of the spend. 

- MEDIA BUYING: I’d plot the frequency of changes made to budgets and target result goals across all campaigns and ad sets - if changes are too infrequent and too large (25-50% swings) I’d 2x change frequency, and 0.5x change sizes to compound improvements. - CREATIVE CHURN: I’d measure creative churn and production vs hit rate. Objective is to identify how fast we run out of new creatives and if our production is meeting hit rate targets. This will let me predict when our ad account will stop producing returns.

Bottom line - to grow active subscribers:

Keep "Total Active Subscriptions" as a North Star if you want, but don't use it to make decisions. Instead break it into it’s components: 

1. Reactive lost subscribers
2. Extend LTV on existing subscribers
3. Acquire new subscribers

I spend $3M/mo on Meta for 8 DTC brands.

How I structure ad accounts: 

ASC:
→ 30% of budget
→ This is for prospecting
→ Once we find a winner in ABO, we move it here to allow Meta’s algorithm to find pockets of efficiency and scale it broadly.
→ This campaign is more passively managed
→ I do not go 100% ASC. I think that is a recipe for disaster if you have multiple products and complex value propositions. 
→ E.g ASC would struggle for an all-natural perfume brand. They have niche customers, multiple scents. ‘Scent’ focused creatives would get mixed with ‘All natural health’ creatives and get served to the wrong buyers. 
→ I’d only go ASC if there was a single hero product to an obvious customer. E.g. A pet brand selling a single unique chew toy for dogs.

ABO: 
→ 70% of budget
→ This is for testing and scaling specific angles.
→ It allows for granular control over specific ad sets.
→ It lets you "override" Meta's algorithm with daily budget management based on performance data that you see, but the algo might miss.
→ Many of our ad sets are inside learning phase. (We don’t care and don’t see it negatively impact performance)
→ Running $2M/mo+ in ABOs requires multiple hours inside the ad account every single day. If your media buyer is unable to spend that much time - you will likely lose money. 

Summary:

1. If you have multiple products, complex value proposition 
→ Go for ABO 70%, ASC 30%

2. If you have a dedicated media buyer 
→ Go for ABO 70%, ASC 30%

3. If you have a single hero product and clear customer and want passive management 
→ Go for 100% ASC 

And overall, follow performance:
1. If ASC is crushing, then scale into it
2. If it’s soft, push into ABO instead

The only time I split out multiple campaigns? 

When the offering is very different (different countries, or drastically different products with different margin profiles)

Every DTC brand needs a 1st customer P&L:

1. Gross Revenue 

→ First-time orders only
→ This is your raw new customer orders
→ This is before any deductions
→ Compare this to your total revenue, it'll show you what % is not returning.

2. Net Revenue
→ Deduct discounts, returns, and refunds.
→ This normalizes for brands forcing gross revenue by discounting
→ E.g. $400k gross minus 30% off sitewide & 12% refund rate = $232k net

3. Gross Margin
→ Deduct COGS from Net Revenue
→ This tells you if the product itself is profitable before any operating costs
→ If this is thin, no amount of marketing efficiency saves you

4. Contribution Margin
→ Deduct shipping, transaction fees, and fulfillment costs
→ This is your per-order profitability before acquisition costs
→ Reminder, this is without any email, SMS, or retention activities

5. Acquisition Contribution Margin
→ Now deduct your Meta ad spend
→ This is the money you're actually making (or losing) acquiring new customers
→ If you're negative here, you're relying on future purchases to break even
→ Don't confuse this with blended contribution margin, this is new customers only

6. Acquisition MER (aMER)
→ Net Revenue divided by ad spend
→ This is the ratio view of step 5
→ No blended MER which hides returning customer revenue inflating the number

Story time:
- We scaled a brand from mid-eight figures to well into the nine figures. 
- One of the key levers outside of media buying and creative was better understanding their first time profitability. 
- Previously, the marketing spend was generic and broad-targeted. So new customer acquisition was incredibly expensive. 
- Facebook knew it was the easiest to just find returning customers to purchase again, and so they were focused on that. 
- When we forced Meta to prioritize new customers, the cost per acquisition was higher, but the cost per new customer acquisition started to decrease. 
- We got recurring customers instead with email, SMS, and subscriptions (effecient & reliable). 
- 6 months later nCAC was lower than previous CAC since Meta was now dialed in and targeting the right (new) people. 

How can you pull this data?
1. Download customer data by new and returning from Shopify
2. Subtract discounts, returns, and shipping costs. 
3. Subtract your COGS from new customers specifically based on the costs of the products, and the fulfillment, and the transaction fees. 
4. Subtract all of your marketing expenses related to acquisition. 
5. Now you know the profitability of your new customer acquisition and how much retention has to regain to break even. 
6. You know how your profitability would change next month if you did or didn't have your marketing spend turned on. 
7. Now you can calculate your churn and your burn rate and project into the future easily

There are 8 ways to attribute Meta ads

1. MER / nCAC
→ MER (Marketing Efficiency Ratio) or nCAC (New Customer Acquisition Cost).
→ It tells you how many new customers did you get? How much revenue? How much did you spend on marketing.
→ MER and nCAC are the only metrics that can't lie to you. Every platform will inflate its own numbers

2. Post-Purchase Surveys
→ "Where did you first hear about us?" on checkout
→ Measures what people remember. I've seen click attribution overvalue lower-funnel across dozens of accounts.
→ I use this for channel-level budget decisions

3. Marketing Mix Modeling (MMM)
→ Uses your historical spend and revenue data to estimate channel contribution. Doesn't need any user-level tracking to work.
→ It tells you where you are on the diminishing returns curve for each channel. Way more useful than just knowing if something's working.
→ I run this monthly or quarterly to gut-check what surveys are telling me

4. Incrementality / Geo-Lift Testing
→ Turn spend on or off by region and measure the impact on sales.
→ Useful if you're in retail
→ Answers "What happens in Dallas when we kill retargeting for 4 weeks?"
→ Quarterly, for the big strategic questions

5. Multi-Touch Attribution (MTA)
→ Triple Whale, Northbeam, Rockerbox. I can see who bought, where they came from, and validate the attribution myself instead of trusting Meta's dashboard.
→ This powers my Account Control Charts (CPA vs Spend). Shows me which ads are efficient but under-scaled and which ones are burning cash.
→ I use this daily for ad-level decisions

6. Platform-Reported Attribution
→ What Meta, Google, TikTok report in their own dashboards
→ I use these for purchase velocity. Compare 1-day vs 7-day vs 28-day windows to understand how fast people convert after seeing an ad.
→ Always compare click-based vs view-through. If most conversions are view-through, your numbers are inflated.

7. GA4 + Server-Side Tracking
→ GA4 defaults to last-click and it's a Google product. I don't use it for attribution decisions.
→ But CAPI and server-side tracking (Elevar, etc.) is non-negotiable. After iOS 14.5 your pixel is missing half the picture. This feeds better data to every other tool on this list.

8. Cohort-Based LTV
→ Meta at $40 CPA with $180 twelve-month LTV beats TikTok at $30 CPA with $95 LTV.
→ Return rate % and purchase frequency are the two I watch closest. They explain most of the LTV gap between channels.
→ Review monthly. Your CPA targets should come from this.

And of the 8, these are the best 3 to start with:
1. MTA (Triple Whale) for which ads to scale or cut
2. Post-purchase surveys for which channels get budget
3. MMM for quarterly validation

When all three point the same direction, I push budget.

The interesting part is when they disagree.

That's where I start digging into the other attribution methods to identify the nuance.

Alternative Meta campaign structure

Use to maximize profit control:

- Meta has a BIG blind spot.
- It doesn't know your LTV or contribution margin.
- It only knows what converts cheapest right now.

Hedge against this by grouping campaigns by unit economics.

Example: Men's gym brand launching new SKUs.

Campaign 1: Flagship product

→ Three flavor variants of the standard whey (chocolate, vanilla, peanut butter)
→ $45 AOV, ~40% contribution margin, $18 gross profit per unit
→ Repeat rate, payback window, and LTV are the same across all three flavors
→ One campaign, one CPA target (~$20). Let Meta pick the winner across flavors.

Campaign 2: Bundle offer (2x the price but 3x profit and better LTV)

→ 1 tub of the flagship protein + free shaker + free creatine tub
→ $90 AOV. The "free" extras cost you ~$5 in COGS but add ~$40 of perceived value
→ ~64% contribution margin, $58 gross profit per order
→ Let's say it's the same customer as Campaign 1.
→ Separate ABO and ASC, CPA ceiling pushed to ~$40 because the margin can absorb it

If you lump both into the same ASC, Meta optimizes for the cheaper purchase if ROAS is the same despite POAS being better on campaign 2. Your bundle looks like a loser, but only because the CPA ceiling it's being measured against is wrong for it.

Media buyer view:
- Meta has clean signal inside each campaign.
- Now, you can scale the bundle without cannibalizing flagship spend, and you can kill a losing flavor without killing the whole launch.

CFO view:
- Margin per campaign is visible and controllable.
- The bundle with 3x the gross profit per order isn't getting starved while Meta chases a $20 CPA on the flagship.
- Each campaign gets measured against its own payback window. A blended window overpays on the cheap product and underpays on the profitable one.

Point is consider business outcomes in your Meta ad account structure too.

→ First-time orders only, before any deductions
→ Compare to total revenue to see what % isn't returning

→ Deduct discounts, returns, and refunds

→ Deduct COGS from net revenue
→ Tells you if the product is profitable before any operating cost
→ If this is thin, no amount of marketing efficiency saves you

→ Deduct shipping, transaction fees, and fulfillment
→ Per-order profit before you spend a dollar acquiring anyone

→ Don't stop at ad spend. Stack UGC, whitelisting and creator licensing, agency fees, affiliate commissions, software
→ $50k in ad spend becomes $67k all-in
→ True cost multiplier: 1.34x your ad spend

6. Acquisition Contribution Margin
→ Subtract the fully-loaded cost from contribution margin
→ Ad-spend-only reads +$2,420. Fully loaded reads -$14,580
→ Negative means you're relying on future purchases to break even

→ Two metrics: fully-loaded aMER and nCAC
→ CPA reads $25. Fully-loaded nCAC is $33.50
→ The platform number understates your real cost by 34%

→ Tracks your running cash position as you acquire
→ At this spend, every new customer costs you $7.29 before retention kicks in

- Break-even ROAS = 1 / 0.60 = 1.67x.

Your blended ROAS reads 2.0x. Your last dollar (marginal) ran at 1.67x. That dollar broke even.

→ On this account a customer costs $33 to acquire ($55 AOV × 60% margin at break-even).

→ Blended MER = Total revenue divided by total marketing spend.
→ This is not double-counted across platforms.
→ If you add $50k to Meta and blended MER barely moves, the channel is not driving incremental sales
→ That next dollar is buying sales you'd have gotten anyway.

→ Holdout: turn a channel off for two weeks and watch blended revenue. If no change = not incremental (or long conversion window, validate with post-purchase questions FIRST). If you ever have a platform go dark accidentally definitely run this test when it does.

→ Check post purchase survey. Aim for 30% response on the first question "How did you hear about us". If you're seeing survey, blended MER and platform data agree then you have an incremental channel you should spend into

4. Follow marginal ROAS down to profitable CPA.

→ Keep feeding the channel while the next dollar clears your profitable CPA (lower than target CPA)
→ The marginal dollar only has to clear profitability, or push your average back over target.

→ 50% iterations. Take a proven winner and tweak one thing.
→ 40% adjacent. Same selling angle, new format.
→ 10% big swings. Net new wildcard concepts.

2. Monthly creative churn

→ 27-35% of spend churns to new ads every month in high volume accounts.
→ You replace a third of your winners to stay flat.

→ 10-15% of new ads hitting your CPA threshold is healthy.
→ 70% of creatives get cut before week 2.

4. Spend concentration

→ Top 1-2% of ads drive around 50% of spend and revenue.
→ If they share one angle, they can fatigue together.

5. Kill or scale zones

→ Scale zone: about 1% of your ads. They drive 50% of revenue. Move budget onto them 20% at a time.
→ Test zone: 65%+ of your ads. Let them spend until they prove out or drop to kill.
→ Kill zone: enough spend to be 90% confident an ad never hits target. Turn it off.

6. Creative vs copy

→ Creative is about 10x more impactful than primary text.
→ Copy is worth testing anyway. Two primary texts on the same creative: $350 CPA vs $200 CPA.

7. Testing budget

→ Target 1 new concept per $10k in monthly spend.
→ Each new ad should get around $3k in spend

8. Hook rate

→ Median across 50+ DTC brands I've tracked: 32%.
→ Target 35%+. The top 25% of brands run 42%+.

9. Winner lifespan

→ Average winner lasts 45-60 days. Top performers run 90+.
→ Keep the creative pipeline 30 days ahead so replacements are live before decline.

Push spend when:
→ You've got a winner holding its CPA below your scale line with confidence of it potentially scaling

Most brands running Meta traffic to Amazon are optimizing for the wrong person.

You can't fire a purchase event from Amazon back to Meta. So the campaign optimizes on the last thing it can see: the outbound click. Meta gets very good at finding people who click Amazon links. It has no idea which of them ever bought.

I've managed $150M+ in Meta spend and this is the worst signal environment I deal with.

Was talking through this with the founders at Jurni, who was willing to share some data on their learnings. Jurni's fix is a "Pre-retail landing experience" sitting between the ad and the PDP.

What the page has to do:

1. Continue the ad, don't restart it. Same hook, same visual, same claim. If the page reintroduces the brand, you've reset the sale.
2. Handle the objection the PDP can't. On Amazon you're one tile in a grid of 40 competitors. The page is the only place you control the comparison.
3. One exit. No nav, no footer, no second offer. One button, deep linked to the right variant and pack size.

Across their beauty and CPG customer set:

- CPA down ~19%
- ROAS up ~26%
- 22% of ad traffic never clicks through to Amazon

That third number is the one people react badly to. A fifth of your traffic dies on the page.

That's the point though. That's low intent traffic getting filtered before it costs you an Amazon session. And now you have two segments you never had: people who clicked through, and people who didn't. Fire the first as your optimization event.

Then it compounds. Higher-intent traffic on the PDP lifts conversion rate, and Amazon's ranking rewards conversion rate. You buy better traffic, and the algorithm hands you cheaper organic placement for it.

Worth noting-  these pages Jurni builds are AI-generated per-audience/per-ad variant, not one static page. That's part of why the objection-handling can be this specific: each version is built to match the exact ad it's continuing, and they're tracking performance per variant, not just in aggregate

Caveat: this is their data across their customers, not mine, and CPA is in-platform. I'd want to see it hold in a geo test before I called it incremental.

I run a Meta/Google ads agency exclusively for (high) 8 & 9-figure brands. I'll be the first to say AEO is IMPORTANT. A quick 101 guide in case you haven't made any changes:

1. Map the buying decisions

→ A buying decision is anything a shopper settles before they buy, across discovery, comparison, objections, fit and care.
→ Pull 20-30 questions from support tickets, reviews, site search and post-purchase surveys, in the shopper's wording.
→ Example: "best polarized sunglasses for driving" (discovery), "[brand] vs [competitor]" (comparison), "is [brand] worth the price" (objection), "will [frames] fit a wide face" (fit), "how to clean [lenses]" (care).
→ Each question is a prompt. Type each prompt word for word into ChatGPT and Google AI Mode more than once. Log the answer, whether you were mentioned or cited, and which sources it pulled.

2. Fix eligibility

→ OpenAI runs 3 crawlers. GPTBot is training, OAI-SearchBot is search inclusion, ChatGPT-User is user-triggered fetches.
→ OpenAI will commit a felony (Hugging Face hack) for training; they may ignore your bots.txt, but I don’t risk it. A broad WAF rule or a wildcard disallow should in theory stop these bots which you don’t want.
→ Robots.txt changes take roughly 24 hours to register on OpenAI's side.

3. Build a product truth layer

→ Put price, availability, variants, shipping and returns in visible HTML. Keep your Merchant Center feed matching the page.
→ Same problem as a Meta catalog throwing disapprovals when the feed and the PDP disagree on price. Same fix, wider blast radius.

4. Publish data only you have

→ Publish return reasons, support questions, product tests and sizing failures.
→ This is the single most underused asset in DTC. Use it for AEO, but also for creative.

5. Answer the follow-up questions

→ AI Mode queries average 3x the length of a traditional search.
→ One decision page should cover the answer, trade-offs, edge cases and next step.

6. Write an honest comparison page

→ Own "X vs Y" with a dated methodology, named criteria, and who shouldn't buy your product.

7. Keep product names consistent

→ Use the same brand, model and variant names everywhere. Otherwise the engine reads your old reviews, new listing and current SKU as 3 unrelated things.

8. Earn corroboration

→ Fix wrong facts on the review sites and forum threads already showing up in your answers from move 1.

9. Land citations on the right page

→ Deep-link citations to the relevant PDP or guide. A great ad pointed at a generic homepage underperforms a mediocre ad pointed at the right page.

10. Measure

→ Track AI visibility in Search Console, AI referrals in analytics, and citation rates on your question set, dated before and after.
→ Add an AI option to your post-purchase survey. When someone asks an assistant and walks straight to your site, there's no click to capture.

Shout out to Lorea Lastiri for this playbook.

I'm not an AEO expert, but she is!

Can you scale on Meta ads?

Plot your aMER versus your blended MER.

Blended MER (bMER) = total revenue divided by total marketing spend.
Acquisition MER (aMER) = new-customer revenue divided by acquisition spend.

Two lines to plot against:
→ Sitting on the bMER = aMER diagonal means no repeat revenue to average in
→ Falling below aMER = 1 means you're buying customers at a loss

Plot yourself and you land in one of four spots.

Low bMER, low aMER
→ E.g. 1.6 bMER vs 0.9 aMER, nCAC $238, below the loss line
→ This is the brand scaling past breakeven. Every new customer costs you more than they're worth right now, and payback stretches past a year
→ Cut the worst 20-30% of spend, reset to the efficient core, rebuild through creative testing

Low bMER, mid aMER
→ E.g. 2.3 bMER vs 2.1 aMER, 10% repeat customers, right on the bMER = aMER line
→ This is the leaky bucket. There's no repeat business to average in, so bMER barely clears aMER
→ Fix retention before you scale spend

High bMER, low aMER
→ E.g. 6.0 bMER vs 1.3 aMER, 78% repeat customers
→ Left alone, Meta harvests the cheapest conversions available, and those conversions are people who were buying anyway
→ Rebuild prospecting with hooks written for cold traffic, accept a lower bMER for a quarter

High bMER, high aMER
→ E.g. 8.4 bMER vs 4.6 aMER, marketing at 12% of revenue
→ This is the brand that's growing too efficiently. You need to spend more!
→ Keep spending until marginal aMER hits your LTV:CAC goal to grow quicker.

I spent 150 million on Meta.

Eight variables make up a winning ad.

Ranked here from least important to most:

1. Audio quality / lighting
→ Phone-shot creator ads beat studio about 80-90% of the time.
→ Polish pays off in luxury, complex demos and some fashion. Everywhere else, shoot on an iPhone in natural light.

2. Ad length / CTA
→ Runtime and CTA wording barely move a result. 15-30 seconds wins most DTC tests.
→ Go long when trust has to come before the product. Founder stories hold the product back until 40-50 seconds, documentary-style testimonials run long, and a proven concept can stretch to 2-5 minutes with more proof. Saw a 13-minute ad at the top of an ad account once.

3. Filming location
→ Location tells the viewer when and where the product gets used. Keep the use case the same and a new setting is a low-impact change.
→ Change the location to go after a different use case. The same product in the kitchen, the bathroom and on the sofa pitches 3 different use cases.
→ If you want to try to drive CPMs down you can pick a weird location to film something, it can work but is a risk.

4. Key selling points
→ The selling point is the reason to buy your product over the one next to it.
→ Find the one USP no competitor claims, then show it visually. A static built on a striking visual of one USP has taken $2M+ on a single ad for one of our clients

5. Offer
→ An offer change hits every impression at once. A strong offer is behind almost every account I've seen scale 2x in a month.
→ Sequence offer tests. An A+ offer can jump this whole list.

6. Creator
→ In my tests only around 20% of creators are compelling, which makes creator one of the biggest swings in any test.
→ If you're testing a new creator, give them 1-2 top ads to remake so the creator is the only new variable. If you're testing anything else, use a top creator who reliably performs.

7. Angle
→ The top 1-2% of ads drive around 50% of spend. If they share an angle, they can fatigue together.
→ Spin a winning angle into 15-20 variations. Keep any one angle under 40% of active spend.

8. Product
→ A new product can change who the ad goes to entirely. And the product is what people spend their money on, so it outweighs everything else on this list.

→ CPMr is the cost to reach 1,000 people, so a low CPMr means the ad finds new people cheaply
→ Bubbles are sized by reach and split at the account's medians into 4 groups
→ Efficient growth is cheap reach with lower CPA
→ Reach play is cheap reach with higher CPA
→ Precision is expensive reach with lower CPA
→ Kill candidate is expensive reach with higher CPA

How I read them together
→ Scale zone + efficient growth ads get scaled more aggressively than my usual 5-15%
→ Scale zone + precision ads go up at the normal pace while I watch that CPA holds as spend climbs
→ Kill zone + reach play ads get a 10-20% bump on target CPA first, since cheap reach often starts buying journeys that close later
→ If a reach play ad hasn't closed the gap after a couple weeks of real spend, I get more conservative
→ Kill zone + kill candidate ads are cut quickly.

STOP wasting money on LTV prediction models

Run this simple test:

1. Take every customer who first bought 90+ days ago
2. Rank them by revenue at day 3
3. Rank the same customers by revenue at day 90
4. Correlate the two rankings

Answer tells you how well day 3 revenue predicts day 90 revenue in your account.

Around 70%:
→ You have a big optimization opportunity
→ Early revenue is not tracking long term value
→ You're probably overbidding on the customers who have low LTV
→ And likely underbidding the slow burn high LTV customers who take a full 90 days to materialize

85% or higher:
→ Leave it alone
→ Day 3 revenue is a good predictor of your LTV

Note - be careful with averages.
- Look for outliers.
- Two brands can post an identical average day 90 revenue and get opposite answers on this test.

Feel free to adjust the day depending on when your repeat purchases occur

I've spent $20M during BFCM

1. Divide your BFCM budget by $3,000

→ Plan one new ad for every $3K of spend.

2026-11-07.text:
Creative is the last thing I look at every day

After $150M+ in ad spend managed, my daily optimization is really just three questions. And I go in order.

1. More or less?
Should the account be spending more or less today? I look at nCAC and budget for that, and I start from total new customers before I split anything out. If nCAC is coming in under target and there's room in the budget, we push. If it's over, we pull back.

2. Into what?
Once that's set, where does the spend go. Usually I split by product, sometimes by campaign, and move it toward whatever's bringing in new customers at the best cost. On a few accounts I'm weighting LTV:CAC by product more than straight CAC.

3. Which creatives?
Only then do I actually open the ads. Push whatever's carrying nCAC and cut what's dragging it down.

Creative still matters a ton obviously. But if the account should be spending less today, no new ad is going to fix that.

2026-11-08.text:
You'll hear a lot that the brand should be in the first frame.

I've run 30,000+ ads and I'd actually start a little more generic.

When the brand is the focus right up front, the ad will probably pull in more people who already know the brand. And it'll convert them, so the numbers can look fine. But they were already familiar with you.

Start with something more generic and you reach people who have a problem. They might not know your name yet, that's fine. If they see their problem in the first few seconds they'll keep watching, and then the brand shows up and you sell them.

For a generic open I'd try the problem itself on screen, or the thing they already tried that didn't work. A question they're already asking themselves works too.

2026-11-11.text:
Build a winning BFCM ad by matching your ad & lander to EXACTLY what's running through a customer's brain:

1. Hook

→ "Wait, what's this?"
→ Call out one person or one problem.
→ Put the same callout in your lander's headline.

2. Event

→ "Oh, it's the sale."
→ Give the discount a reason, like a holiday or your own sale name.
→ Run the same sale name in the lander banner.

3. Offer

→ "How much off?"
→ Show one number, readable in a second, then say what it covers.
→ Show the same offer above the fold, and again at add to cart.

4. Hero

→ "What is it, exactly?"
→ Show the product, in use if it needs explaining.
→ Keep the lander to that one product.

5. Math

→ "Is that actually a deal?"
→ Turn the % into dollars.
→ Tell the shopper on the lander what they pay and what they save.

6. Proof

→ "Is it any good?"
→ Put a number on trust, like a review count.
→ Test pulling reviews above the buy box, so shoppers read them before you ask for money.

7. Clock

→ "Can I wait till Cyber Monday?"
→ Name the day the sale ends.
→ Run an active timer on the lander, so the end date is clear.

8. Close

→ "How do I get it?"
→ Take out the last step.
→ Put the code at the top of the lander. Most shoppers will be on mobile.
